football_evidence.question: Can Texas Tech contain Cincinnati’s explosive runs?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Texas Tech, and its own breakdown accounts for about 0.0 of the 3.2 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Texas Tech has the ball (big plays on the ground): Texas Tech’s offense turns 10.1% of its runs into explosive gains, and Cincinnati’s defense gives up explosive gains on 7.8% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).

When Cincinnati has the ball (big plays through the air): Cincinnati’s offense turns 10.2% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Texas Tech’s defense gives up explosive gains on 7.3% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.3%).

When Cincinnati has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Cincinnati’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 17.9% of its runs, and Texas Tech’s defense stops 21.7% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.3%).

When Texas Tech has the ball (early downs): Texas Tech’s offense succeeds on 51.7% of its first- and second-down plays, and Cincinnati’s defense allows success on 44.0% of first- and second-down plays (FBS average 42.7%).
contradicting: When Cincinnati has the ball (the passing game against the pass defense): Cincinnati’s offense averages 9.1 yards per pass attempt, and Texas Tech’s defense allows 7.1 yards per pass attempt (FBS average 7.4).
